title: World Bank Small AI for Development Hackathon 2026: Build Inclusive AI Solutions and Win Sponsored Travel to Seoul
summary: Applications are open for the World Bank Group Small AI for Development Hackathon Challenge 2026 , a global innovation opportunity inviting young people to develop practical artificial intelligence solutions for communities and economies facing limited connectivity, infrastructure and access to digital technology. Participants will compete during a two-day hackathon on 3–4 October 2026 , developing a working “Small AI” solution addressing a real development challenge in one of three sectors: Health Agriculture Tourism Three winning entries will be selected, with one winner representing each sector. The winners will be invited to present their solutions at the Global AI and Digital Summit 2026 , taking place from 19–22 October 2026 in Seoul, Republic of Korea . The final deadline to apply for the hackathon is 26 September 2026 . Applications and all competition submissions must be completed in English. Key Information at a Glance Programme: Small AI for Development Hackathon Challenge 2026 Related event: Global AI and Digital Summit 2026 Hackathon dates: 3–4 October 2026 Hackathon format: Hybrid, with online participation and physical hubs Application deadline: 26 September 2026 Summit dates: 19–22 October 2026 Summit location: Grand Hyatt, Seoul, Republic of Korea Winner presentations: 21 October 2026 Challenge sectors: Health, agriculture and tourism Application language: English Team size: Individual applications or teams of up to four people Number of World Bank challenge winners: Three Competition partner: Hack-Nation Referral code: WBGSmallAIGADS Application form: Apply through the official Google Form Official information: Global AI and Digital Summit 2026 The application form currently requires applicants to sign in to Google. Candidates should therefore ensure that they have access to an active Google account before starting. About the Small AI for Development Hackathon Challenge The Small AI for Development Hackathon is organized by the World Bank Group’s Digital and AI Vice Presidency in collaboration with the World Bank Group Youth Summit, Development Economics Vice Presidency and Information and Technology Solutions. Hack-Nation is responsible for managing the competition platform and administering the hackathon process. The World Bank Group serves as the sponsor and final judging authority. The challenge is intended to encourage artificial intelligence development that responds to the actual conditions experienced in developing economies. Instead of assuming that every user has reliable broadband, an advanced smartphone and strong digital literacy, participants must consider environments where access to technology remains constrained. The organizers are looking for solutions that can translate artificial intelligence into practical development outcomes rather than demonstrations of technology without a clearly defined problem or target user. Why This Challenge Matters The competition has been launched against the backdrop of significant global connectivity and employment challenges. According to the official World Bank event page, more than two billion people remained offline as of 2025. At the same time, approximately 1.2 billion young people in the Global South are expected to reach working age during the coming decade, while current trends indicate that substantially fewer jobs will be created. Artificial intelligence may support economic growth, better services and new employment opportunities. However, many existing AI applications have been designed for environments with advanced devices, dependable internet connectivity and users who already understand how to communicate with AI systems. This challenge asks young innovators to reconsider those assumptions and create technology that can function under real development constraints. What Is “Small AI”? Small AI is a targeted and use-case-driven approach to artificial intelligence development. Unlike general-purpose AI systems that require extensive computing and data-centre infrastructure, Small AI focuses on using specific capabilities to solve a clearly defined problem. A Small AI solution may operate through accessible technologies such as: Basic mobile phones Sensors Microcontrollers Locally operated models SMS-based interfaces Voice-based systems Devices with limited processing capacity Systems that function with intermittent or restricted connectivity A solution may use predictive, generative or agentic AI. The decisive issue is not the size or complexity of the model but whether the technology addresses a real problem within the operating environment of its intended users. Effective Small AI solutions should be designed around: A specific development problem Clearly identified users Local data and knowledge Limited or unreliable connectivity Affordable and accessible devices Familiar communication channels Measurable development outcomes Responsible and inclusive implementation Realistic infrastructure and institutional conditions The World Bank also stresses that Small AI still depends on enabling foundations such as broadband access, digital literacy and trusted local institutions. Without these foundations, even technically promising solutions may remain isolated pilots instead of becoming sustainable and scalable interventions. Challenge Areas Every applicant must select one of the three official sector challenges. Health Applicants selecting health must develop an AI solution that responds to the relevant development challenge and operating conditions identified in the official sector brief. Solutions will need to demonstrate how Small AI can contribute practical value in contexts where communities may face limitations in connectivity, devices, infrastructure, information or access to services. Agriculture Agriculture applicants must consider how targeted AI applications can create measurable value for agricultural stakeholders in resource-constrained environments. The proposed technology should be grounded in a specific problem and should account for the digital tools, data, infrastructure and institutional conditions that must be present for the solution to work. Tourism Applicants selecting tourism must develop a practical solution that responds to the official tourism-sector challenge. The proposal should show how AI can produce meaningful benefits within the sector while remaining accessible, context-specific and realistic about connectivity and technology constraints. Applicants should consult the official sector briefs and avoid attempting to address all three sectors in one entry. The World Bank’s rules require each entry to respond to one sectoral challenge. What Participants Must Build The hackathon requires participants to build a working Small AI solution during the official competition weekend. The proposed solution should: Address one clearly defined challenge in health, agriculture or tourism. Operate within the realities of a constrained environment. Demonstrate a clear advantage over existing approaches. Produce measurable or credible development value. Consider accessibility and inclusion. Reflect local needs, users and operating conditions. Explain the infrastructure and preconditions required for implementation. Acknowledge relevant technical, social and development trade-offs. Comply with the technical and submission rules published by Hack-Nation. Be submitted through the official competition platform during the prescribed window. The broader Hack-Nation programme describes the event as a 24-hour global building experience delivered online and through physical hubs. Participants are expected to move from identifying a problem to developing and presenting a working AI product. Application Rounds and Final Deadline Hack-Nation is processing applications through several batches: Application batch Deadline Batch 1 8 August 2026 Batch 2 22 August 2026 Batch 3 5 September 2026 Batch 4 12 September 2026 Batch 5 19 September 2026 Batch 6 26 September 2026 The World Bank Group identifies 26 September 2026 as the final application deadline. Candidates should apply during the earliest remaining batch rather than waiting until the final deadline. Applying to the hackathon does not automatically constitute a valid competition entry and does not guarantee acceptance or eligibility for judging. How to Apply Participation involves two separate and mandatory stages. Step 1: Apply for the Hackathon Applicants must complete the official Hack-Nation application process by 26 September 2026 . The direct application form is: Small AI for Development Hackathon 2026 Application Form Applicants may also visit the Hack-Nation Hackathon 7 page , select “Apply” and enter the following referral code: WBGSmallAIGADS The application must be submitted in English. Applicants should understand that submitting this initial form only applies for admission to the hackathon. It is not the final competition submission. Step 2: Develop and Submit the Competition Entry Registered and accepted participants must develop their Small AI solution during the official hackathon window on 3–4 October 2026 . The final entry must be submitted through the designated Hack-Nation competition portal and comply with all published requirements concerning: Submission deadline Technical format Team composition Originality Challenge selection Demonstration materials Video submission Use of the referral code English-language requirements Intellectual-property compliance Only entries formally submitted and confirmed as received through the official competition platform will be considered for judging. Applications or entries submitted through email, social media, messages to World Bank Group staff or unofficial channels will not be accepted. Late, incomplete or incorrectly submitted entries will not be considered. Rules for Individual and Team Participation Applications may be made individually or as a team of up to four members. For team applications: Every team member must register individually. Every member must independently satisfy all applicable requirements. All members must identify themselves as belonging to the same team before the application deadline. A participant may be associated with only one competition entry. Team membership cannot be changed after the hackathon begins. A team submission will be evaluated as one entry. A winning team will collectively receive one of the three winning places. A winning team must nominate one member to represent it in Seoul. The World Bank Group judging panel will make the final determination regarding the traveling representative. Teams should finalize their membership, roles and sector selection before submitting their applications. How Entries Will Be Evaluated Hack-Nation will evaluate eligible entries and prepare a shortlist for the World Bank Group. The World Bank Group will then act as the final judging authority and select the three winners. Entries will not be assessed solely on technical sophistication. The organizers will also consider: Development relevance Quality of problem definition Suitability for constrained environments Measurable potential impact Design quality Accessibility Inclusivity Practicality Local relevance Responsible use of AI Awareness of infrastructure requirements Recognition of trade-offs Potential for implementation or expansion Applicants are encouraged to explain what localized AI development means within their particular setting. They should demonstrate how their perspective or direct understanding of a local challenge has shaped the proposed solution. The organizers are interested in entries that recognize tensions between technological capability and accessibility, as well as between ambition and responsible risk management. Competition Timeline Milestone Date Final application deadline 26 September 2026 Hackathon and competition-entry window 3–4 October 2026 Winner notification and preparation 5–6 October 2026 Winning representatives travel to Seoul By 18 October 2026 Global AI and Digital Summit 19–22 October 2026 Winner presentations at the Summit 21 October 2026 Selected winners must be prepared to respond quickly after notification because the period between the hackathon and travel to Seoul is short. What the Three Winners Receive Three winners will be selected: One winner from agriculture One winner from health One winner from tourism Each winning entry will be featured through a high-impact presentation during an appropriate sector session at the Global AI and Digital Summit. The organizers will determine: Presentation format Length of the presentation Session placement Presentation requirements The individual who will speak for a winning team Winners may also be offered facilitated meetings with: Investors Private-sector representatives Micro, small and medium-sized enterprises Government officials International development stakeholders Other Summit participants Such meetings are subject to availability and mutual interest and should not be treated as guaranteed. Travel and Accommodation Support The World Bank Group states that reasonable travel, accommodation and designated event-related expenses will be covered for the selected winning individuals or approved team representatives traveling to Seoul. Applicants should carefully note the following conditions: Only the selected individual or one approved representative of a winning team will travel. The organizers will determine which expenses are reasonable and eligible. Travel support is linked to participation in required Summit activities. Winners remain responsible for obtaining the necessary visa. Visa application fees and related costs are not automatically covered. The World Bank Group cannot guarantee, influence or accelerate immigration decisions. A letter of support will be provided after the winning entry is confirmed. Winners should begin the visa process immediately after notification. The organizers are not liable if a selected winner cannot obtain a visa. An alternate winner may be selected if the original winner cannot travel or participate. Hack-Nation separately advertises more than US$35,000 in cash and technology credits across its broader Hackathon 7 programme. The World Bank page does not specify what portion of that general prize pool, if any, is allocated to this particular Small AI challenge. Applicants should therefore rely only on the World Bank’s expressly stated Seoul presentation and travel benefits unless Hack-Nation confirms additional awards. About the Global AI and Digital Summit 2026 The Global AI and Digital Summit is a high-level forum hosted by the World Bank Group together with the Republic of Korea’s Ministry of Finance and Economy and Ministry of Science and ICT. It will take place from 19–22 October 2026 at the Grand Hyatt in Seoul . The Summit will examine how artificial intelligence and digital transformation can help countries: Generate more and better jobs Raise productivity Expand economic opportunity Improve public services Strengthen businesses Develop trusted digital ecosystems Expand affordable digital access Build AI readiness Mobilize investment Deliver practical development outcomes The programme will bring together government leaders, development partners, private-sector executives, investors, technology innovators, researchers, civil-society representatives and youth leaders. In-person participation in the Summit is by invitation only. Selected sessions will be open to the public and streamed online, with livestream information expected as the programme is finalized. Overview of the Summit Agenda The official Summit agenda remains subject to change. Monday, 19 October 2026 The opening day will include Summit registration, an invitation-only ministerial meeting, a ministerial luncheon and a welcome reception. The ministerial meeting will involve World Bank Group and Korean government leadership and will focus on high-level digital and AI priorities. Tuesday, 20 October 2026 The second day will focus on enabling the AI economy and creating or transforming jobs. Programme areas include: Financing digital and AI infrastructure Converting digital ambitions into investable projects Small AI and its development impact Universal connectivity in the AI era Exhibition and networking activities Decisions about what elements of the AI technology stack countries should build, share or purchase Digital trust and protection of critical infrastructure Development of AI ecosystems and agents Cross-border data and trust Partnerships capable of scaling locally relevant AI solutions Some infrastructure and investment discussions will be closed and available only to invited participants. Wednesday, 21 October 2026 The third day will focus on scaling practical AI solutions for development. Discussion areas include: Private investment for affordable digital access AI-ready infrastructure AI opportunities in developing economies Health applications The resource and infrastructure costs of AI Digital public infrastructure and government service delivery Device affordability Digital transformation at subnational level Common reasons digital transformation programmes stall Frontline AI applications AI-supported growth in agriculture and tourism The Republic of Korea’s AI and digital-development experience The Small AI challenge winners are scheduled to present their solutions on this day. Thursday, 22 October 2026 The closing day is expected to include study tours and consultations with participating clients and stakeholders. Intellectual Property and Submission Rights Participants retain ownership, copyright and other rights in their entries. However, submission of an entry grants the World Bank Group a worldwide, non-exclusive and royalty-free licence to: Review and evaluate the submission Reproduce relevant materials Display or record the submission Publish summaries Present the solution publicly Use the entry for competition administration Use materials for educational, promotional and knowledge-sharing purposes Participants must possess all rights necessary to submit their materials. Entries must not knowingly violate another party’s: Copyright Trademark Privacy Confidentiality Intellectual property Contractual rights Applicants should document the sources of datasets, code, models, images, audio, research and other materials used in their solution. Restrictions on World Bank and Partner Branding Participants may not independently place the names, titles, acronyms, logos or branding elements of the World Bank Group or its partners on their entry materials without prior written consent. This restriction also covers branding associated with: Hack-Nation World Bank Group Youth Summit Development Economics Vice Presidency Information and Technology Solutions Other programme partners Applicants should describe the challenge accurately without creating materials that imply official endorsement, partnership or organizational approval beyond what has been expressly authorized. Data Protection Information submitted during registration and the hackathon may be shared with the World Bank Group, Hack-Nation and relevant stakeholders involved in: Competition administration Hosting Participant coordination Judging Winner notification Summit participation Follow-up communication Personal data will be handled in accordance with the World Bank Group Privacy Notice . Applicants should review the privacy terms of both the World Bank Group and the external application or competition platforms before providing personal information. Other Important Conditions By participating, applicants accept the official competition terms and acknowledge that: The organizers may verify compliance at any stage. Ineligible candidates may be disqualified. Incomplete or non-compliant entries may be removed. The organizers are not responsible for lost, late, corrupted or misdirected submissions. Illegal or rights-infringing content may be excluded. Final decisions concerning judging and winner selection rest with the organizers. The competition may be modified, suspended, shortened, cancelled or terminated. An alternate winner may be selected if a winner is ineligible, unavailable or unable to participate. The privileges and immunities of the World Bank Group remain reserved. Submissions must not be used for purposes inconsistent with the World Bank Group’s mandate and mission. Participants should read the complete terms on the official event page rather than relying only on promotional summaries. Practical Application Advice Applicants can strengthen their preparation by taking the following actions: Apply during the earliest available batch. Form the complete team before registration. Confirm that every team member registers individually. Select only one official sector challenge. Study the relevant sector brief. Define one specific user and problem. Identify the actual connectivity, device and data constraints. Explain why AI is necessary for the solution. Build around locally available technology. Define measurable indicators of impact. Incorporate accessibility and inclusion from the beginning. Prepare a realistic working prototype rather than an overly broad concept. Plan the demonstration and video submission early. Verify all intellectual-property permissions. Avoid unauthorized World Bank or partner logos. Monitor the World Bank and Hack-Nation pages for updates. Keep evidence that both the application and final entry were successfully submitted. Ensure that a potential team representative could travel to Seoul at short notice. Application Deadline The final deadline to apply is: 26 September 2026 The official page does not specify a deadline time or time zone. Applicants should submit well before the final date. The actual competition entry must subsequently be developed and submitted during the official hackathon window on 3–4 October 2026 . Application and Reference Links Official World Bank information: Global AI and Digital Summit 2026 and Small AI Hackathon Challenge Direct application form: Apply through the official Google Form Competition platform: Hack-Nation Global AI Hackathon 7 Referral code: WBGSmallAIGADS For general information about the Global AI and Digital Summit, contact GADS@worldbankgroup.org . Due to the anticipated volume of applications, the organizers state that they cannot respond individually to questions concerning competition eligibility, application status or judging results. Applicants should monitor the official World Bank and Hack-Nation pages for announcements. Conclusion The World Bank Group Small AI for Development Hackathon Challenge 2026 provides young innovators with an opportunity to rethink how artificial intelligence can serve people living and working in environments with limited connectivity, devices and digital infrastructure. The strongest entries will not necessarily be the largest or most technically complex. Successful solutions will need to address a well-defined health, agriculture or tourism challenge, demonstrate measurable development value, respond to local realities and function through accessible technology. Three winners will earn the opportunity to present their work at the Global AI and Digital Summit in Seoul, with reasonable travel, accommodation and designated participation expenses covered under the organizers’ conditions. Prospective applicants should apply early, finalize their teams, review the relevant sector challenge and prepare for an intensive development and submission period on 3–4 October 2026. title: JICE Japan-Africa Youth Program 2026: Fully Funded Japan Visit for African Animation Professionals
summary: The JICE Japan-Africa Youth Program – Professionals Japan Visit Program for Co-creation (Animation Production) offers African animation professionals an opportunity to travel to Japan for an approximately 12-day international exchange and professional learning experience focused on animation production, industry exposure, networking, cultural exchange, and collaboration. Organized by the Japan International Cooperation Center (JICE) as part of the Japan-Africa Youth Program , the initiative is designed to bring together African animation professionals and Japanese anime creators, companies, organizations, and educational institutions. For selected participants, program participation and travel expenses are free of charge , making this a significant opportunity for professionals seeking international exposure and connections within Japan s globally influential animation industry. The application deadline is Tuesday, September 8, 2026, at 23:59 Japan Standard Time (JST) . About the JICE Japan-Africa Youth Program The Japan-Africa Youth Program is an international exchange initiative promoted by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan and implemented as part of efforts to strengthen mutual understanding and relationships between young people from Japan and Africa. The broader program focuses on allowing young people from both regions to learn from one another through direct interaction, observation, cultural experiences, and professional exchange. The Professionals Japan Visit Program for Co-creation (Animation Production) forms part of this wider initiative and focuses specifically on professionals working in Africa s animation industry. The program recognizes the growing importance of animation and anime as creative industries capable of connecting cultures, creating economic opportunities, developing talent, and encouraging international collaboration. Through the Japan visit, African participants will have the opportunity to gain first-hand exposure to Japan s animation ecosystem while building relationships with Japanese professionals and organizations. What Is the JICE Professionals Japan Visit Program for Co-creation? The Professionals Japan Visit Program for Co-creation (Animation Production) is an international exchange and professional development initiative specifically designed for African animation professionals. JICE plans to invite 20 individuals working at anime production companies in Africa to Japan for approximately 12 days . Rather than being simply a tourism or cultural visit, the program is structured around professional exposure, networking, learning, cultural exchange, and the development of future partnerships between African and Japanese animation stakeholders. Participants are expected to explore Japan s anime production environment and learn more about the country s animation-related industries and educational institutions. The program also aims to create opportunities for African participants to connect directly with Japanese companies and creators, potentially laying the groundwork for future cooperation and co-creation. Key Objectives of the Program The initiative has several interconnected objectives. 1. Strengthen Japan-Africa professional networks One of the central goals is to establish stronger relationships between animation professionals from Africa and Japan. By bringing professionals together in Japan, the program provides an environment where participants can exchange ideas, discuss industry developments, identify areas of mutual interest, and explore potential future collaboration. 2. Increase exposure to Japan s animation industry Japan has an internationally recognized anime and animation ecosystem. The visit is intended to provide African professionals with an opportunity to experience aspects of this ecosystem directly, including exposure to animation production sites, related industries, companies, and educational institutions. This type of first-hand experience can provide insights that may be difficult to obtain through online research alone. 3. Encourage co-creation The program is specifically framed around co-creation , meaning that the goal is not simply for African professionals to observe Japan s animation sector. Instead, the initiative seeks to encourage relationships through which professionals from both regions can exchange ideas and potentially develop future projects together. This makes networking and relationship-building important components of the experience. 4. Promote cultural understanding Participants will also have opportunities to deepen their understanding of Japanese culture, values, mindset, and cultural heritage. At the same time, interaction between African and Japanese participants can contribute to greater awareness of Africa s own creative industries and cultural perspectives. 5. Support future African leaders The broader Japan-Africa Youth Program seeks to empower young people to become leaders capable of contributing to Africa s future development. For animation professionals, this means combining professional development with international exposure and intercultural exchange. What Will Participants Experience in Japan? The program is expected to last approximately 12 days , during which selected participants will take part in activities connected to animation, professional exchange, and cultural learning. Although the exact itinerary should be confirmed in the official Draft Standard Itinerary and Application Guidelines, the announcement indicates that participants will have opportunities to explore: Anime production sites. Animation-related industries. Japanese animation companies and organizations. Educational institutions connected to the animation sector. Japanese cultural and social environments. Professional networking opportunities. Cultural exchange activities. Discussions and interactions with Japanese creators and industry stakeholders. The program is therefore particularly relevant to professionals who want to understand how Japan s animation ecosystem operates and how African and Japanese creative professionals could collaborate. Who Is the Program Looking For? The call is specifically aimed at African anime creators and professionals working within anime production companies or organizations in Africa . JICE intends to accommodate 20 participants in total . However, the application structure is particularly important. Applications are being sought from interested companies and organizations , with participation limited to a maximum of 10 companies in total . Each participating company can send no more than two individuals . The two participants are expected to consist of: One company executive The first participant should be a company executive who will act as the decision-maker . This role is important because the program is designed to encourage organizational and business-level collaboration in addition to individual professional development. One creative professional The second participant should be a creative professional working in the animation field. This allows the program to bring both organizational decision-making perspectives and hands-on creative expertise into the Japan-Africa exchange. Geographic Eligibility: Who Can Apply? The opportunity is specifically targeted at Africa . JICE describes the initiative as targeting African anime creators , and the program is intended for young professionals in the animation industry from Africa. Therefore, professionals and organizations operating within the African animation sector should pay particular attention to this opportunity. However, the announcement provided does not list every eligible African country individually . Applicants should therefore consult the official Application Guidelines to confirm whether their specific country, organization, and professional circumstances meet all requirements. In other words, the opportunity has a clear Africa-wide focus , but applicants should not assume that every organization automatically qualifies without checking the detailed guidelines. How Many Participants Will Be Selected? The program intends to invite 20 individuals to Japan. At the organizational level: Up to 10 companies or organizations can participate. Each company can nominate a maximum of two participants . The two participants should include a company executive/decision-maker and a creative professional. This structure means that the program is not simply seeking 20 unrelated individual applicants. It is designed to engage animation companies and organizations and facilitate meaningful professional connections between African and Japanese stakeholders. Major Benefits of the JICE Japan Visit Program Participating in the JICE Japan-Africa Youth Program can offer several professional and personal advantages. 1. Fully Covered Program Participation and Travel Expenses One of the most significant benefits is that participation in the program and travel expenses are free of charge . This can substantially reduce the financial barrier associated with participating in an international professional exchange program. However, applicants should carefully distinguish between expenses covered by the program and personal expenses that remain their responsibility. 2. International Exposure Selected professionals will travel to Japan and gain direct exposure to one of the world s most influential animation ecosystems. This can broaden their understanding of: Animation production. Creative industry structures. Professional practices. Industry collaboration. Animation-related education. Cultural influences on creative production. Potential international partnerships. 3. Networking With Japanese Animation Professionals Networking is one of the core elements of the initiative. Participants will have opportunities to interact with Japanese animation creators and related organizations. For African animation professionals, these relationships could potentially contribute to future: Partnerships. Creative collaborations. Knowledge exchange. Business relationships. Co-production opportunities. Professional networks. The program is particularly valuable for professionals interested in building connections beyond their domestic markets. 4. Exposure to Animation Production Sites Participants are expected to have opportunities to discover Japanese anime production sites and related industry environments. First-hand exposure can help professionals understand how animation projects are developed, produced, managed, and supported within Japan s creative ecosystem. 5. Access to Animation-Related Institutions The program also intends to expose participants to animation-related industries and educational institutions . This can be useful for professionals interested in understanding the relationship between education, skills development, creative production, and the commercial animation sector. 6. Cross-Cultural Learning The program is also designed to deepen participants understanding of Japan s: Values. Mindset. Culture. Cultural heritage. Social systems. At the same time, participants bring their own African professional and cultural experiences into the exchange. This creates a two-way learning process rather than a one-sided study visit. 7. Potential for Future Co-Creation The concept of co-creation is central to the program. African and Japanese animation professionals can use the exchange to identify shared interests and explore ways of working together. Although participation should not be interpreted as a guarantee of future contracts, funding, employment, or commercial partnerships, the relationships developed during the program may provide a foundation for future collaboration. What Expenses Are Covered? According to the announcement, participation in the program and travel expenses are free of charge . This is an important feature of the opportunity for professionals who may otherwise face significant international travel costs. However, not every expense is covered. Expenses participants are responsible for Participants are specifically expected to cover personal expenses, including: Transportation between their home and the airport. Passport issuance fees. Other personal expenses not covered under the program. Applicants should therefore avoid interpreting free of charge as meaning that absolutely no personal expenditure will be required. The official Application Guidelines should be reviewed carefully for the complete list of covered and non-covered costs. Application Documents Required JICE has provided several documents that applicants should review before completing the application. These include: 1. Application Guidelines The Application Guidelines contain the detailed requirements, instructions, and conditions governing the application process. 2. Letter of Understanding Applicants should also review the Letter of Understanding to understand the commitments and conditions associated with participation. 3. Handling of Personal Information This document explains the handling of personal information associated with the program and application process. 4. Draft Standard Itinerary The Draft Standard Itinerary provides applicants with an indication of the expected structure and activities of the Japan visit. Applicants are strongly encouraged to read all four documents before submitting an application. How to Apply for the JICE Japan-Africa Youth Program Interested companies and organizations should complete the official online application process. The application requires applicants to provide the information requested through JICE s online application system. Applicants should ensure that all required information is prepared before starting or completing the online form. Important Application Warning JICE has issued an important warning concerning the online application system. If applicants spend an extended period completing the form, the application may not be submitted properly . To reduce this risk, JICE strongly recommends preparing written responses and other text in a separate word-processing document before entering the information into the online application form. A practical approach would be to: Read the Application Guidelines completely. Identify every question requiring a written response. Draft responses in Microsoft Word or another word processor. Proofread all responses. Gather the required information. Open the official application form. Copy and paste prepared responses into the relevant sections. Review the completed form carefully. Submit the application well before the deadline. Confirm that the submission has been completed successfully. This approach can also reduce the risk of losing carefully prepared information if the online form session expires. Application Deadline for the JICE Japan-Africa Youth Program The application deadline is: Tuesday, September 8, 2026, at 23:59 Japan Standard Time (JST). Applicants should pay close attention to the time zone. The online application system will automatically close at 23:59 JST , meaning applicants should not wait until the final minute to submit their applications. Because applicants are based across Africa and may be operating in different time zones, it is advisable to convert the deadline into local time and submit the application considerably earlier. For applicants in Kenya, for example, Japan Standard Time is ahead of East Africa Time, so the application should be submitted before the equivalent local deadline rather than relying on the date alone. Selection Process and Notification of Results According to JICE, the results are expected to be announced in early October 2026 . However, this schedule is tentative and may change depending on the number of applications received. Applicants should therefore monitor communications from JICE after submitting their applications. The announcement does not state that all eligible applicants will automatically be selected. Given the limited number of available places—20 participants—the application should clearly demonstrate why the applicant and their organization are appropriate for the program. How to Prepare a Strong Application Because the number of participants is limited, applicants should approach the application strategically. 1. Understand the purpose of the program Before applying, applicants should understand that this is not simply a tourism opportunity. The program is designed around: Professional exchange. Animation industry exposure. Japan-Africa relations. Networking. Cultural understanding. Co-creation. Future collaboration. Applications should therefore demonstrate genuine professional interest in these areas. 2. title: Gandel Foundation Annual Open Grant Program 2026: Up to $50,000 for Organisations Supporting Young People’s Positive Futures in Australia
summary: Applications will soon open for the Gandel Foundation Annual Open Grant Program 2026 , offering eligible Australian charitable organisations the opportunity to apply for funding of up to $50,000 for projects lasting up to one year . The 2026 Annual Open Grant Program is focused on Young People’s Positive Futures , with funding intended to support organisations helping young adults aged 16 to 24 navigate significant transitions in their lives, particularly young people experiencing multiple and interconnected forms of disadvantage. The grant round seeks to support organisations that help young people overcome barriers to: Wellbeing Social participation Education Employment Economic engagement Community participation Independence Positive life transitions Particular attention is given to young people facing circumstances such as: Poverty Homelessness Substance use Trauma Health challenges Leaving out-of-home care Exiting the justice system Finishing formal education Transitioning into employment Other complex barriers to participation and independence Importantly, this funding opportunity is not available directly to individual young people . Applications must come from eligible organisations registered with the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission (ACNC) and holding Deductible Gift Recipient (DGR) Item 1 status at the time of application. The grant process involves two stages. Organisations must first submit an Expression of Interest (EOI) . Selected organisations will then be invited to submit a full application. The EOI round opens on: Friday, 11 September 2026 at 9:00 AM and closes on: Thursday, 1 October 2026 at 12:00 PM midday EOI applicants are expected to receive notification of the first-stage outcome on: Wednesday, 7 October 2026 Eligible organisations are encouraged to review the Gandel Foundation’s FY26–29 Strategy , Grant Guidelines and Funding Exclusions before preparing an application. About the Gandel Foundation Annual Open Grant Program The Gandel Foundation provides philanthropic support to organisations seeking to create positive social outcomes in Australia. Many of the Foundation’s other grant opportunities are primarily proactive or invitation-based. However, the Annual Open Grant Program provides an opportunity for eligible organisations to apply through an open competitive process. For the current round, the Foundation has selected: Young People’s Positive Futures as the central funding focus. The programme recognizes that the period between adolescence and adulthood can be particularly significant. For many young people, the years between 16 and 24 involve major transitions involving: Education Employment Housing Independence Relationships Community participation Financial responsibility Health Identity Interaction with public institutions Young people who have access to stable support systems may be able to navigate these transitions successfully. Others, however, may encounter significant barriers. The Annual Open Grant Program is designed particularly to support organisations working with those young people whose transitions toward adulthood are complicated by disadvantage. Focus of the 2026 Grant Round: Young People’s Positive Futures The 2026 Annual Open Grant Program focuses specifically on: Young adults aged 16–24 who are moving through significant developmental and life transitions. Gandel Foundation recognizes that this period can shape a young person’s future trajectory. The right support during an important transition may help a young person: Remain connected to education Find meaningful employment Maintain stable housing Build supportive relationships Improve wellbeing Participate in society Avoid re-entry into the justice system Develop greater independence Build confidence and skills The programme therefore seeks organisations capable of providing meaningful, appropriately timed support. Priority for Young People Experiencing Multiple Disadvantages The grant programme particularly emphasizes young people experiencing: Multiple and interconnected forms of disadvantage. This distinction is important. The Foundation is not only interested in addressing a single isolated barrier. Some young people may simultaneously experience combinations of: Financial hardship Unstable housing Family disruption Trauma Mental or physical health challenges Substance use Justice-system involvement Educational disengagement Limited employment opportunities Social exclusion When several barriers overlap, the transition to independent adulthood can become significantly more difficult. The grant programme therefore prioritizes organisations supporting particularly vulnerable and marginalized young people. Supporting Young People Experiencing Poverty Poverty can affect multiple areas of a young person’s life. Financial insecurity may make it harder to: Continue studying Travel to education or employment Maintain stable accommodation Participate socially Access services Prepare for employment Meet basic needs Projects seeking to improve young people’s longer-term pathways may therefore address economic barriers alongside broader social and developmental needs. Supporting Young People Experiencing Homelessness Young people facing homelessness or unstable accommodation may encounter significant barriers to education, employment, health and social participation. Organisations working with homeless or housing-insecure young people may potentially fit the objectives of the programme where their work supports positive transitions and longer-term outcomes. The Foundation’s focus is on helping young people navigate barriers that prevent them from realizing their potential. Supporting Young People Affected by Trauma Experiences of trauma can have long-term effects on: Mental health Education Relationships Employment Trust Decision-making Participation in community life The programme recognizes trauma as one of several factors that can contribute to interconnected disadvantage. Organisations supporting trauma-affected young people may therefore be relevant where their programmes align with the wider goal of building positive future pathways. Health Challenges Health challenges are also identified as one of the possible forms of disadvantage affecting young adults. These may interact with: Housing insecurity Economic participation Education Employment Social engagement The programme’s broader approach recognizes that barriers affecting young people are often interconnected rather than neatly separated. Substance Use The Foundation also acknowledges that substance use can form part of the complex circumstances affecting young people’s transition toward adulthood. Organisations addressing substance use alongside broader issues of wellbeing, employment, housing or social participation may therefore potentially align with the programme’s priorities. Transition From Out-of-Home Care One important transition explicitly highlighted by Gandel Foundation is: Leaving out-of-home care. Young people leaving care may face major changes in: Housing Financial responsibility Education Employment Support networks Access to services Independent living The move from structured care arrangements toward independent adulthood can be particularly difficult where stable family or community support is limited. The programme therefore welcomes organisations helping young people make this transition successfully. Young People Exiting the Justice System Another transition specifically identified is: Exiting the justice system. Young people leaving the justice system may encounter barriers involving: Employment Education Housing Social stigma Family relationships Community participation Re-engagement with services Support during this period may help create stronger pathways toward stability and social participation. Organisations working with young people transitioning out of justice-system involvement may therefore find the grant particularly relevant. Transition From Education The Foundation also highlights young people who are: Finishing formal education. The transition out of school, vocational education or another educational setting can be challenging, especially when young people lack clear pathways into: Employment Further study Training Community participation Programmes that help vulnerable young people move from education into sustainable next steps may align with the funding focus. Transition Into Employment Employment can be a major element of the transition into adulthood. Yet young people experiencing multiple disadvantages may encounter barriers including: Limited work experience Educational disruption Lack of professional networks Housing instability Health problems Justice-system involvement Financial hardship Projects that help young people navigate the transition into employment may be suitable where they contribute to broader wellbeing and economic engagement. Grant Amount The Annual Open Grant Program offers grants of: Up to $50,000 for projects lasting: Up to one year The supplied information does not explicitly label the currency as AUD, although the Foundation and programme operate in Australia. Applicants should confirm the exact financial terms in the official Grant Guidelines before finalizing budgets. The maximum grant amount should also not be interpreted as an automatic award of $50,000 to every successful applicant. Applicants should develop a budget appropriate to the actual scale and needs of their proposed project. Grant Duration Funding is available for: Up to one year This means applicants should develop projects that can reasonably deliver their proposed activities and outcomes within a 12-month period. A strong project should therefore have: Clearly defined objectives Realistic activities Appropriate staffing Measurable outcomes A realistic budget A practical implementation timeline Two-Stage Application Process The Gandel Foundation Annual Open Grant Program uses a: Two-stage application process This is important because organisations do not initially submit the full grant proposal. The process begins with an: Expression of Interest or: EOI Only organisations selected during the first stage will be invited to move to the second stage. Stage 1: Expression of Interest The EOI allows the Foundation to identify organisations and project concepts that best align with: The programme’s focus Eligibility requirements Strategic priorities Funding objectives Organisations should use the EOI to communicate clearly: The problem they are addressing The young people they serve The transition point involved The disadvantages faced by the target group The proposed response Why the intervention matters The outcomes expected Applicants should avoid trying to include every possible organisational activity. The EOI should focus specifically on the project being proposed for this grant round. Stage 2: Full Application Following assessment of the EOIs, selected applicants will be: Invited to submit a full application. Being invited to Stage 2 does not necessarily guarantee funding. Rather, it means the organisation has progressed to a more detailed assessment stage. The full application is likely to require additional information about areas such as: Project design Budget Outcomes Implementation Organisational capacity Evaluation Applicants should follow the instructions supplied to shortlisted organisations. EOI Opening Date EOI submissions open on: Friday, 11 September 2026 at 9:00 AM The online application portal will become available through the Gandel Foundation website when submissions open. Organisations cannot submit the formal EOI before the application period begins. EOI Deadline EOI submissions close on: Thursday, 1 October 2026 at 12:00 PM midday Applicants should pay close attention to the closing time. The deadline is midday , not midnight. Organisations should aim to submit in advance to avoid: Portal issues Internet problems Missing attachments Last-minute revisions EOI Outcome Date Organisations are expected to receive notification of their first-stage outcome on: Wednesday, 7 October 2026 Those invited to continue will then move into the full application stage. Who Can Apply? The programme is designed for: Eligible charitable and not-for-profit organisations rather than individuals. Two organizational eligibility requirements are specifically identified. Applicants must: Be registered with the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission. Hold Deductible Gift Recipient Item 1 status when applying. Both requirements are important. Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission Registration Applicants must be registered with the: Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission commonly known as: ACNC Organisations that are not registered with the ACNC do not meet the published eligibility requirements. Applicants should check their registration status before beginning the application. DGR Item 1 Status Organisations must also hold: Deductible Gift Recipient Item 1 status at the time of application. This is a specific tax status relevant to eligible Australian charitable organisations. Holding general not-for-profit status without DGR Item 1 status is not sufficient under the stated criteria. Applicants should verify this before preparing an EOI. Individuals Cannot Apply The Gandel Foundation explicitly states: Individuals cannot be funded. This means the programme is not a direct grant for: Individual young people Students Young entrepreneurs Researchers Individual community leaders Young people aged 16–24 are the intended beneficiaries of funded programmes , not the direct grant applicants. The application must come from an eligible organisation. One Application Per Organisation The Foundation will accept: No more than one application per organisation. Organisations operating multiple programmes must therefore decide which proposed project best aligns with the grant round. Submitting several applications under different teams or projects is not allowed under the published rules. This makes internal prioritization important. Geographic Focus The programme supports work across Australia, but geographic preferences apply. The Foundation states that: Preference is given to Victorian organisations and programmes. This means organisations and projects based in: Victoria, Australia may receive particular consideration. However, organisations outside Victoria are not automatically excluded. Organisations Outside Victoria The Foundation may consider organisations outside Victoria if they: Have a national focus, or Address a broader community issue This creates potential eligibility for organisations operating elsewhere in Australia where the project has relevance beyond a narrowly local context. Applicants outside Victoria should explain clearly why their work fits the Foundation’s broader priorities. Funding Exclusions Before submitting an EOI, organisations should carefully review the Foundation’s general funding exclusions. Several important exclusions apply. No Funding for Individuals The Foundation does not fund individual applicants. All applications must come from qualifying organisations. No Retrospective Funding The Foundation will not provide: Retrospective funding This means organisations should not apply for expenses that have already been incurred or projects that have already been completed. The grant should support future activity. No Recurrent Administrative Costs The Foundation does not provide funding for: Recurrent administrative costs Applicants should therefore distinguish between the direct costs of delivering the proposed project and the organisation’s ongoing general operating expenses. Applicants should consult the detailed Grant Guidelines for clarification about allowable project-related overheads or staffing. No Continuous Funding Gandel Foundation states that it does: Not provide continuous funding to organisations. Applicants should therefore not design the proposal around the assumption that funding will automatically continue after the one-year grant period. Projects should have a clear plan for sustainability or completion. No Duplicate Services The Foundation will not fund programmes that: Duplicate existing services. Applicants should therefore demonstrate what is distinctive about their proposed intervention. They should be able to explain: What gap currently exists Why existing services do not adequately address it How the proposed programme adds value No Auspiced Applications The Foundation does not accept: Auspiced applications. An organisation cannot therefore rely on another entity to apply as its auspicing body. Applicants need to meet the Foundation’s eligibility requirements themselves. Government Bodies Are Not Eligible The Foundation does not provide grants to: Government bodies. This is important for: Government departments Local government entities Public agencies Applicants should verify their institutional status before applying. Harmful Activities Are Excluded Funding will not be provided for activities that may be considered harmful to: Community Environment This aligns with the Foundation’s broader philanthropic and social-impact objectives. Personal Expenses Are Not Funded The Foundation does not fund: Personal expenses. The grant is intended for eligible organisational programmes rather than personal financial support. Films and Documentaries Are Usually Not Funded Gandel Foundation states that it does not usually fund: Film production Documentary production Organisations proposing media-focused projects should therefore review this exclusion carefully before investing time in an application. Review the FY26–29 Strategy Before Applying The Foundation strongly encourages applicants to review its: FY26–29 Strategy before submitting an EOI. This is strategically important. A competitive application should not simply meet the formal eligibility criteria. It should also demonstrate alignment with the Foundation’s broader priorities. Applicants should use the strategy to understand: What Gandel Foundation aims to achieve Which communities it prioritizes How it understands social impact What kinds of interventions align with its approach Review the Grant Guidelines Applicants should also carefully read the: Annual Open Grant Program Guidelines before beginning the EOI. The guidelines should be treated as the authoritative source regarding: Eligibility Application requirements Funding conditions Assessment Project expectations Organisations should avoid relying only on social-media summaries. Review Funding Exclusions Before preparing the application, applicants should confirm that neither their organisation nor proposed activities fall within one of the Foundation’s exclusions. This can save significant time. A compelling project will not proceed if the organisation does not meet the fundamental funding rules. Building a Strong EOI 1. Clearly Identify the Young People You Serve Do not describe the target group simply as: “Young people aged 16–24.” Explain who they are. For example: Young people leaving care Young people experiencing homelessness Young people transitioning out of justice-system involvement Young people disconnected from education Young people facing several overlapping disadvantages The more clearly the target population is understood, the easier it is to evaluate the project. 2. Explain the Transition Point The programme is particularly focused on transitions. A strong application should identify: What transition is taking place? For example: Care to independent living Justice system to community reintegration School to employment Education to further study Homelessness to stable housing Trauma recovery toward social participation This helps demonstrate direct alignment with the funding theme. 3. Explain the Barriers The Foundation specifically emphasizes multiple and interconnected disadvantage. Applicants should describe the barriers experienced by participants. These might include combinations of: Poverty Housing instability Trauma Health challenges Substance use Educational exclusion Employment barriers Avoid treating disadvantage only as a generic label. 4. Explain What Will Change A grant proposal should describe outcomes rather than only activities. Instead of saying: “We will deliver workshops,” explain what those workshops are expected to achieve. Potential outcomes might involve improvements in: Wellbeing Social participation Employment readiness Education engagement Stable housing Confidence Independence The exact outcomes should be appropriate to the proposed programme. 5. Demonstrate That the Programme Does Not Duplicate Existing Services The Foundation explicitly excludes duplicated services. Applicants should therefore explain: What existing services are available What gap remains Why the proposed approach is necessary How the programme complements rather than duplicates existing support 6. Develop a Realistic One-Year Plan Because funding is available for up to one year, the proposed programme should be achievable within that period. A strong plan should clearly establish: Start-up activities Participant engagement Service delivery Monitoring Evaluation Final outputs Avoid proposing an overly ambitious intervention that cannot realistically be delivered within 12 months. 7. Build a Justified Budget The maximum available funding is: $50,000 but applicants should request what is genuinely required. A credible budget should connect directly to: Project activities Staffing Participant support Delivery expenses Evaluation Relevant project costs subject to the Foundation’s funding rules. What Makes This Grant Different? The Annual Open Grant Program is particularly notable because Gandel Foundation states that many of its other grants are predominantly: By invitation only. The Annual Open Grant Program therefore creates a more accessible entry point for qualifying organisations that may not already have an invitation-based funding relationship with the Foundation. However, the programme remains competitive and targeted. Applicants should demonstrate both: Formal eligibility Strong strategic alignment Important Dates at a Glance EOI applications open: Friday, 11 September 2026 at 9:00 AM EOI applications close: Thursday, 1 October 2026 at 12:00 PM midday EOI outcome notification: Wednesday, 7 October 2026 Full application stage: By invitation following successful EOI assessment Important Funding Details at a Glance Funder: Gandel Foundation Programme: Annual Open Grant Program 2026 focus: Young People’s Positive Futures Target beneficiaries: Young people aged 16–24 Maximum grant: Up to $50,000 Grant duration: Up to one year Application process: Two stages Stage 1: Expression of Interest Stage 2: Full application by invitation Number of applications: Maximum one per organisation Geographic preference: Victoria, with some consideration for eligible organisations outside Victoria with national or broader community focus Eligibility Checklist Before applying, organisations should confirm that they: Are registered with the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission.
